questions.q: Why can a security architecture that looks maximally secure on paper produce worse real-world outcomes?
options: Usability has no real effect on how securely people actually behave
Maximum restriction is always the most secure option in every real scenario
This only happens in organizations with no helpdesk
When legitimate access is too restricted, users don't stop working -- they find workarounds outside the governed system that are less secure than the control itself
questions.explain: Friction drives people toward workarounds that live outside the system's audit trail and controls entirely -- a strictly worse outcome.

questions.q: Why is a shared login worse than the over-broad individual role it replaces?
options: Shared logins are actually more secure because fewer accounts exist
It has no real effect on auditability
It eliminates individual accountability and the audit trail entirely, rather than just granting slightly more access than necessary
ServiceNow blocks shared logins automatically, so this never happens
questions.explain: An over-broad role at least has an identifiable owner; a shared login has none, which is a strictly worse security posture.

questions.q: What is a "shadow export," and why is it a security failure despite starting from a security-motivated restriction?
options: A feature that doesn't exist in ServiceNow
An export that is actually more secure than in-platform access
A scheduled, approved report exported through official ServiceNow channels
A user exporting data to a personal spreadsheet because in-platform access is too restricted -- the export has no ACLs, audit log, or encryption at all
questions.explain: The restriction that was meant to protect the data instead pushes it into an ungoverned file with none of the original controls.

questions.q: What is the real architectural judgment this lesson describes, as opposed to applying maximum restriction everywhere?
options: Letting each team independently decide its own security posture with no standard
Removing all access controls so no workaround is ever needed
Applying the exact same restriction level to every table regardless of sensitivity
Being genuinely strict where risk justifies it, and genuinely frictionless everywhere else, rather than uniform maximum restriction across the whole instance
questions.explain: Risk-proportionate friction keeps the genuinely sensitive data tightly controlled while removing the user's reason to work around everything else.

questions.q: What early signal should a Technical Architect look for to catch this problem before it becomes shadow IT?
options: A drop in overall instance uptime
An increase in the number of scheduled maintenance windows
A decrease in the number of approved ACLs on the instance
Spikes in data exports from sensitive tables, helpdesk requests for someone else's login, or a department running an unofficial duplicate tracker
questions.explain: These are the upstream symptoms of a friction problem, and the fix is redesigning access -- not a policy-compliance reminder.
